name: Elkhorn Coral
flavor: A formation of Elkhorn Coral erupts from the ground, broad calcium plates fanning outward like antlers of stone.
fun_facts: One of the most important reef-building corals in the Caribbean, forming dense thickets that shelter hundreds of fish species.
Its broad, flattened branches resemble elk antlers and can grow up to 2 meters wide.
Listed as critically endangered — populations have declined over 90% since the 1980s.
Reproduces by both fragmentation (broken branches regrow) and mass annual spawning events.
Colonies can live for centuries and grow up to 2.5 cm per year.

name: Staghorn Coral
flavor: A thicket of Staghorn Coral branches upward in a violent surge, its antler-like arms forming a jagged barrier of calcified bone.
fun_facts: Named for its resemblance to deer antlers, it forms dense thickets called thicket reefs.
One of the fastest-growing corals, extending up to 10-20 cm per year under ideal conditions.
Critically endangered and protected under the US Endangered Species Act since 2006.
Often hybridizes with elkhorn coral to produce a third species, Acropora prolifera.
Provides critical nursery habitat for juvenile reef fish including grouper and snapper.

name: Millepora Coral
flavor: Millepora Coral blooms into existence, a thousand tiny pores opening across its pink-tinged surface like eyes awakening from slumber.
fun_facts: A highly variable species found across the Indo-Pacific in colors ranging from cream to bright pink and purple.
One of the most studied corals in bleaching research due to its sensitivity to temperature changes.
Individual colonies can change sex from year to year — sequential hermaphroditism.
Its name means thousand pores, referring to the tiny polyp openings covering its surface.
A key species in coral restoration programs across Australia's Great Barrier Reef.

name: Plate Coral
flavor: A wide disc of Plate Coral unfurls like a shield of living stone, its flat expanse casting shade across the battlefield below.
fun_facts: Forms large, flat table-like structures up to 2 meters across that act as platforms for resting reef fish.
The flat shape is an adaptation to maximize light capture in deeper, lower-light environments.
Fish like hawkfish and dottybacks shelter beneath the plate and dart out to feed.
Extremely vulnerable to crown-of-thorns starfish predation, which can consume an entire plate overnight.
Colonies fragment during storms, and broken pieces can reattach and continue growing.

name: Lobe Coral
flavor: A colossal boulder of Lobe Coral heaves upward from the earth, centuries of layered growth compressed into a single moment of conjuration.
fun_facts: Forms massive boulders that can be over 8 meters tall and hundreds of years old.
Its skeleton acts as a natural climate record — scientists drill cores to study past sea temperatures.
One of the most thermally tolerant corals, often surviving bleaching events that kill neighboring species.
Home to dozens of boring organisms like sponges, worms, and bivalves that tunnel into its skeleton.
Found from Hawaii to the Red Sea, making it one of the most geographically widespread corals.

name: Finger Coral
flavor: Thick digits of Finger Coral thrust up from the stone, grasping at the air like the hand of something vast buried beneath.
fun_facts: Forms dense colonies of thick, finger-like branches that create important shelter for reef fish.
Extremely common in Hawaii, where it is a dominant reef-builder in many bays.
Can survive in turbid, low-salinity conditions that would kill most other corals.
Colonies may live for more than 500 years, recording centuries of ocean history in their skeletons.
Provides nesting substrate for Hawaiian dascyllus (humbug damselfish) which vigorously defend their patch.

name: Mustard Hill Coral
flavor: A dome of Mustard Hill Coral rises with quiet resilience, its golden surface humming with the warmth of symbiotic life.
fun_facts: One of the most resistant Caribbean corals — it often outlasts other species during bleaching events.
Its distinctive mustard-yellow color comes from symbiotic zooxanthellae algae living in its tissue.
Forms small, dome-shaped colonies rarely exceeding 30 cm, but can live for decades.
One of the few coral species appearing to increase in abundance as climate change winnows competitors.
Spawns in late summer, releasing bundles of eggs and sperm during nighttime mass spawning events.

name: Great Star Coral
flavor: Great Star Coral congeals into a massive boulder, each polyp a wide staring eye that pulses with emerald fluorescence.
fun_facts: Features some of the largest polyps of any Caribbean reef coral — individual polyps can be over 1 cm wide.
Colonies can form massive boulders weighing several tonnes and living for centuries.
At night, its large tentacles extend dramatically to feed on plankton and small organisms.
One of the dominant framework-building corals on Caribbean deep reef slopes from 15-50 m depth.
Exhibits fluorescence under blue light, glowing vivid green or orange due to fluorescent proteins.

name: Boulder Star Coral
flavor: An ancient mound of Boulder Star Coral solidifies from raw magic, growth rings spiraling through its skeleton like the memory of eight hundred winters.
fun_facts: Historically the most important reef-building coral in the Caribbean.
Individual colonies can grow into mounds over 2 meters tall and may be more than 800 years old.
Growth rings in the skeleton, like tree rings, allow scientists to read annual growth rates.
Experienced catastrophic bleaching during the 1998 and 2005 mass bleaching events.
The species complex was recently split into three distinct species based on genetic analysis.

name: Grooved Brain Coral
flavor: A massive Grooved Brain Coral materializes, its labyrinthine grooves pulsing with ancient thought as if the sea itself were dreaming.
fun_facts: Its convoluted ridges and valleys look uncannily like a human brain — the pattern is called meandroid.
The maze-like pattern is formed by colonies of polyps that share a common mouth groove.
Can live for more than 900 years, making it among the longest-lived animals on the planet.
One of the few Caribbean corals that spawns in pulses over multiple nights after the full moon.
The grooves channel mucus away from the coral surface, helping to self-clean sediment and debris.

name: Symmetrical Brain Coral
flavor: Symmetrical Brain Coral coalesces with eerie precision, its perfectly ordered ridges suggesting a mind of geometric perfection.
fun_facts: Distinguished from other brain corals by its especially regular, symmetrical meandroid pattern.
Prefers shallower, well-lit reef zones where its zooxanthellae can photosynthesize efficiently.
During bleaching stress, it can expel its zooxanthellae and take months to recover.
Colonies grow very slowly — sometimes less than 5 mm per year in diameter.
A common target for parrotfish, which scrape off the outer tissue while feeding on algae.

name: Boulder Brain Coral
flavor: A titanic Boulder Brain Coral crashes into being, its deep valleys carved like canyons across a thinking stone the size of a carriage.
fun_facts: One of the largest brain corals — boulders can reach 2 meters in diameter and weigh several tonnes.
Its wide, deep valleys distinguish it from other Caribbean brain corals.
Can survive partial colony death — sections of the boulder may bleach and die while others survive.
Important as a spawning aggregation landmark for many reef fish species.
Studies show it can acclimate to warmer temperatures over multiple bleaching events.

name: Golfball Coral
flavor: A small but impossibly dense sphere of Golfball Coral snaps into existence, deceptively diminutive yet harboring decades of stubborn life.
fun_facts: One of the smallest Caribbean reef corals, rarely exceeding 10 cm in diameter.
Despite its small size, it can live for decades on shallow rocky and sandy substrates.
One of very few corals that broods its larvae internally rather than broadcasting eggs into the water.
The brooded larvae are released already containing their symbiotic zooxanthellae algae.
Tolerates a wider range of salinity and turbidity than most other Caribbean hard corals.

name: Closed Brain Coral
flavor: Closed Brain Coral emerges as a tightly sealed mosaic of fused polyps, its walls locked together like the cells of an armored vault.
fun_facts: The polyps are closed — adjacent corallites share walls, creating a tightly packed mosaic pattern.
Widespread across the Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea to French Polynesia.
A hardy species often found in turbid inshore reef environments that other corals avoid.
Feeds nocturnally, extending tentacles to capture zooplankton in the water column.
Used as an indicator species in reef health assessments due to its sensitivity to sedimentation.

name: Goniastrea Coral
flavor: Goniastrea Coral spreads across the ground in a rounded mass, its net-like surface radiating heat-hardened resilience.
fun_facts: Forms rounded, encrusting colonies with a distinctive net-like retiform surface pattern.
One of the most thermally tolerant corals on the Great Barrier Reef.
Studies have shown it can harbor heat-tolerant strains of zooxanthellae that help it survive bleaching.
Colonies are important substrate for settling coral larvae, facilitating reef recovery after disturbance.
Has been found living in naturally warm, extreme reef environments like the Persian Gulf.

name: Galaxea Coral
flavor: Galaxea Coral crystallizes into a field of tiny skeletal tubes, each polyp a distant star in a constellation of venomous light.
fun_facts: Each polyp sits in its own separate skeletal tube, giving the colony a galaxy-like starfield appearance.
Extremely aggressive — it extends long sweeper tentacles at night to sting and kill neighboring corals.
One of the most popular corals in the marine aquarium trade, prized for its otherworldly appearance.
Colonies can grow very large, sometimes covering several square meters of reef.
Its mucus contains compounds being researched for potential antifungal and antibacterial properties.

name: Yellow Scroll Coral
flavor: Vivid yellow plates of Scroll Coral curl into being like parchment unfurling, each convoluted fold a sheltering alcove of calcified gold.
fun_facts: Forms distinctive scroll-like, convoluted plates that maximize surface area for light capture.
Its vivid yellow color is unusual among corals and makes it highly recognizable underwater.
The scrolled shape creates sheltered microhabitats used by small fish, shrimp, and cryptic invertebrates.
Grows in deeper, lower-light reef zones where its large surface area helps it photosynthesize.
Popular in reef aquariums but slow-growing and sensitive to water quality changes.

name: Cactus Coral
flavor: Sharp vertical ridges of Cactus Coral jut upward like the spines of a petrified desert plant, brittle and forbidding.
fun_facts: Forms large, upright plates with sharp vertical ridges resembling the spines of a cactus.
Widespread in the Indo-Pacific, particularly common in the Maldives and Red Sea.
The ridged structure increases surface area and helps direct water flow over the polyps.
Often forms massive colonies several meters tall on exposed reef slopes.
The thin plate edges are brittle and frequently broken by storms, but fragments can reattach and regrow.

name: Pavona Coral
flavor: Great leaf-like plates of Pavona Coral sweep into form, their criss-crossed ridges catching an unseen current as they harden mid-sway.
fun_facts: Forms large, foliose (leaf-like) plates that sweep dramatically in reef currents.
One of the few corals found at depths exceeding 40 meters in the mesophotic zone.
The criss-cross pattern of ridges on its surface is unique among reef corals.
Often hosts commensal shrimp and small gobies that live exclusively on its surface.
Has been documented recovering quickly from bleaching events compared to branching corals.

name: Leptoseris Coral
flavor: Paper-thin plates of Leptoseris Coral materialize from shadow, so fragile they seem spun from darkness itself yet rigid as bone.
fun_facts: A specialist of deep, low-light reef environments, found from 30-150 meters depth.
Its extremely thin, fragile plates are optimized for capturing the tiny amount of light available at depth.
Found in the mesophotic zone, a poorly studied coral ecosystem between 30-150 m depth.
Recent deep-reef surveys have discovered new Leptoseris species previously unknown to science.
Unlike shallow corals, mesophotic Leptoseris colonies are rarely affected by surface bleaching events.

name: Mushroom Coral
flavor: A solitary disc of Mushroom Coral drops onto the ground, a single enormous polyp that shifts and rights itself with eerie autonomy.
fun_facts: One of the few solitary (single polyp) corals — the entire disc is one giant polyp.
Free-living as an adult: it can slowly move across the seafloor using its tentacles.
Juveniles are attached to the substrate, but adults detach and live as mobile discs.
Can right itself if flipped upside down by inflating tissue on one side and deflating the other.
Its large central mouth can engulf prey items much larger than typical coral polyps can consume.

name: Button Mushroom Coral
flavor: Hundreds of tiny Button Mushroom Corals scatter across the ground like coins tossed by a giant, each one a perfect calcified disc.
fun_facts: A tiny free-living coral rarely more than 3-4 cm across, resembling a small button.
Like other fungiids, it can move slowly across sandy substrate to escape burial.
Populations on sandy slopes can be surprisingly dense — hundreds of individuals per square meter.
Can survive burial under sediment by inflating its tissue to push sand away.
Its skeleton has been used in archaeology — ancient Pacific cultures traded fungiid skeletons.

name: Tongue Coral
flavor: An elongated Tongue Coral slithers into view, its many mouths running along a central groove like a creature that speaks in whispers.
fun_facts: An elongated, tongue-shaped free-living coral that can grow up to 30 cm long.
Has multiple mouths running along a central groove down its length.
Lives on sandy or rubble substrates and can slowly migrate across the seafloor.
One of the most recognizable corals due to its unusual elongated shape.
Found from the Red Sea to the central Pacific, usually in sheltered lagoon environments.

name: Feather Coral
flavor: A great Feather Coral takes shape, its elongated septa fanning outward in delicate ridges that belie the weight of its stony body.
fun_facts: A free-living fungiid coral with numerous elongated septa giving it a feathery appearance.
Can grow up to 50 cm across — one of the largest solitary corals in the world.
Multiple mouths run along the tops of its raised ridges.
Hosts commensal shrimp (Periclimenes spp.) that live exclusively on its surface.
Despite being a single polyp, its colony-like appearance confused early taxonomists.

name: Lobed Brain Coral
flavor: Lobed Brain Coral surges forth in fleshy, brilliantly colored lobes, each one retracting and swelling independently like a creature drawing breath.
fun_facts: Forms large, domed or flat colonies with fleshy, lobed polyps in brilliant colors including red, green, and brown.
Extremely aggressive, extending long sweeper tentacles to attack neighboring corals at night.
Popular in the aquarium trade for its dramatic colors and relatively hardy nature.
Each lobe can retract independently, giving the colony a dynamic, changing appearance.
Widespread across the Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea to Australia and Japan.

name: Open Brain Coral
flavor: An Open Brain Coral inflates on the sand, its wrinkled tissue blooming in vivid reds and greens like a wound that refuses to close.
fun_facts: A free-living solitary coral with dramatically fleshy, wrinkled tissue in vivid reds, greens, and blues.
Can inflate its tissue with water to appear much larger than its skeleton.
One of the most sought-after corals in the marine aquarium trade.
Found on sandy and muddy substrate in sheltered lagoons, not typically on hard reef.
Its tissue contains fluorescent proteins that glow vividly under blue or UV light.

name: Maze Brain Coral
flavor: Maze Brain Coral locks into place with deep, winding valleys carved through its dome, a labyrinth no creature could solve.
fun_facts: Forms large flat or domed colonies with deep, wide valleys in a complex maze pattern.
The name recta refers to the relatively straight valley walls compared to other brain corals.
Can survive partial bleaching with sections recovering while others remain bleached.
The fleshy tissue between ridges is home to tiny commensal crabs and shrimp.
Uses sweeper tentacles up to 10 cm long at night to defend territory from neighboring corals.

name: Echinopora Coral
flavor: Thin spiraling plates of Echinopora Coral layer atop one another, building a delicate fortress of overlapping leaf-like stone.
fun_facts: Forms thin, leaf-like plates that spiral and overlap to form complex three-dimensional structures.
The delicate plates provide shelter for a huge variety of small reef organisms.
Can shift between plating and branching growth forms depending on light and water flow.
One of the few corals documented recovering rapidly after physical damage from boat groundings.
Widespread across the Indo-Pacific, particularly abundant on upper reef slopes in the Coral Triangle.

name: Chalice Coral
flavor: A broad Chalice Coral rises like a cup offered to the deep, its rough surface bristling with tiny spines that catch the faintest light.
fun_facts: Forms broad, chalice-shaped or flat plates with rough (aspera = rough) surface texture.
Highly prized in the reef aquarium hobby for vivid multicolored varieties called ultra chalice.
A low-light specialist, naturally found on shaded vertical faces and overhangs.
The rough texture is caused by tiny spines (spinules) on its skeletal elements.
Feeds primarily at night, extending tentacles to capture passing zooplankton.

name: Oxypora Coral
flavor: Oxypora Coral tears itself into being, its ragged lace-like edges fluttering as though freshly ripped from the fabric of the sea.
fun_facts: Forms thin, frilly plates with ragged, lace-like edges — lacera means torn or ragged.
Often found in areas of moderate water flow where its delicate plates can flutter in currents.
The thin plate structure is brittle but grows rapidly, allowing quick recovery from breakage.
Hosts a characteristic community including small gobies and snapping shrimp.
Vibrant aquarium varieties range from cream and green to vivid orange and red.

name: Antler Coral
flavor: Towering plates of Antler Coral branch and twist skyward, a crown of calcified fronds worthy of some primordial forest king.
fun_facts: Forms tall, upright plates that branch and twist to resemble antlers or leafy sea vegetation.
One of the most architecturally complex corals, creating dense three-dimensional reef structures.
The large surface area of its plates supports a diverse community of epibionts.
Prefers sheltered, turbid reef environments rather than exposed high-energy zones.
Listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List due to habitat loss and bleaching.

name: Horn Coral
flavor: Horn Coral bristles into form, its surface studded with pointed projections like the hide of some armored beast readying for war.
fun_facts: Named for the distinctive pointed projections (hydnophores) that stud its surface like tiny horns.
Forms encrusting, massive, or branching colonies depending on environmental conditions.
Extremely aggressive — can digest tissue from neighboring corals on contact.
The horn-like projections house the polyps, which extend at night to feed.
Fast-growing and resilient, it can dominate reef sections after disturbances.

name: Ruffled Ridge Coral
flavor: Ruffled Ridge Coral cascades outward in frozen waves of stone, its ridge-and-valley pattern resembling a tempest captured in calcium.
fun_facts: Forms spectacular ruffled plates with ridge-and-valley patterns resembling ocean waves frozen in stone.
One of the most visually striking corals on Indo-Pacific reefs.
Plates can reach over a meter across in sheltered conditions.
A key indicator species for Indo-Pacific reef health assessments.
The ruffled edges are fragile and often show grazing scars from parrotfish and surgeonfish.

name: Mountainous Star Coral
flavor: Mountainous Star Coral ascends in a columnar dome, its wide corallites glinting like facets on a monument built over centuries.
fun_facts: One of the dominant framework-building corals on Caribbean deep forereefs from 5-30 m.
Distinguished from related species by its larger corallites averaging 5-6 mm.
Forms large, domed or columnar colonies that can live for several hundred years.
Part of the Montastraea annularis complex — only recently recognized as a distinct species.
Participates in mass spawning events in the Caribbean each fall.

name: Massive Starlet Coral
flavor: A smooth, rounded boulder of Massive Starlet Coral settles into place, its pitted star pattern an unshakable testament to endurance.
fun_facts: One of the hardiest Caribbean corals — survives in turbid, silty conditions other corals cannot tolerate.
Forms smooth, rounded boulders with a distinctive pitted star pattern on its surface.
Can grow at depths from 1 m to over 70 m, one of the widest depth ranges of any Caribbean coral.
Notably resistant to bleaching — some colonies survived the 2005 Caribbean bleaching event without bleaching.
Grows slowly, about 4-5 mm per year, so large boulders represent centuries of growth.

name: Blushing Star Coral
flavor: Blushing Star Coral flushes into view, its polyps flaring a vivid orange-red as though startled by its own sudden arrival.
fun_facts: Named blushing because the polyps turn bright orange-red when disturbed or stressed.
Forms small, rounded colonies on shallow Caribbean reefs, rarely exceeding 30 cm.
One of the few Caribbean corals with colonies that are almost perfectly hemispherical.
Its polyps are among the most sensitive to touch, retracting instantly when contacted.
Often overlooked on surveys but provides important substrate for encrusting organisms.

name: Maze Coral
flavor: Maze Coral weaves itself from raw stone, its winding ridges and valleys forming a dense puzzle no blade could easily cleave.
fun_facts: Forms a complex maze of ridges and valleys — meandros is Greek for winding.
One of only a handful of Caribbean corals with a true meandroid skeletal structure.
Its skeleton is extremely dense and heavy compared to branching corals of the same size.
Produces chemical compounds that deter fish grazing — more resistant to predation.
Common on both shallow and deep Caribbean reefs, found from 1-50 m depth.

name: Rough Cactus Coral
flavor: Rough Cactus Coral claws its way into existence with fierce, spiny ridges that promise pain to any hand foolish enough to touch them.
fun_facts: Forms broad, flat colonies with very rough, spiny ridges — ferox means fierce or wild.
One of the most distinctive Caribbean corals, easily identified by its coarse texture.
Found mainly on deep forereef slopes from 20-50 m depth.
Reproduces by brooding larvae internally, releasing swimming juveniles ready to settle.
Listed as threatened under the US Endangered Species Act.

name: Sinuous Cactus Coral
flavor: Sinuous Cactus Coral ripples into form, its wavy undulations rolling across the surface like sand dunes frozen in limestone.
fun_facts: Forms low, flat colonies with wavy, sinuous ridges giving a distinctive undulating surface.
Found on shallow Caribbean reefs from 1-20 m depth.
One of the few Caribbean corals that frequently shows natural color variation: green, brown, and grey.
Broods its larvae internally and releases them as swimming planulae at night.
Often shares substrate with encrusting algae, sponges, and other sessile invertebrates.

name: Spiny Flower Coral
flavor: Spiny Flower Coral unfolds its enormous fleshy polyps in a riot of crimson and emerald, each one a bloom that could swallow a coin whole.
fun_facts: Has extraordinarily fleshy, colorful polyps — among the most dramatic-looking of all Caribbean corals.
Tissue colors include vivid reds, oranges, greens, and yellows.
A relatively rare coral on modern reefs, listed as threatened under the US Endangered Species Act.
Lives on deeper Caribbean reefs from 10-50 m, avoiding the shallow wave-disturbed zone.
Each corallite (polyp cup) can be up to 3 cm wide, making individual polyps visible to the naked eye.

name: Smooth Flower Coral
flavor: Clusters of Smooth Flower Coral project outward like trumpets of bone, their sweeper tentacles already uncoiling to claim the surrounding ground.
fun_facts: Has uniquely elongated corallites that project outward from the colony like clusters of trumpets.
Occurs as both solitary and colonial forms on Caribbean reefs.
Produces one of the longest sweeper tentacles of any Caribbean coral — up to 15 cm.
Often found on deep forereef slopes and under ledges in shaded environments.
Broods its larvae internally for extended periods before releasing them as fully formed juveniles.

name: Pillar Coral
flavor: Towering columns of Pillar Coral erupt skyward, their polyps visibly writhing in daylight as though the pillars themselves were alive and restless.
fun_facts: Grows in spectacular upright columns that can exceed 2 meters in height — unmistakable on any reef.
Polyps are unusual in being active during the day, with tentacles visibly extended in daylight.
Critically endangered — pillar coral populations have declined by over 80% in recent decades.
Reproduces extremely slowly, making recovery from population crashes very difficult.
Listed as threatened under the US Endangered Species Act and protected in many Caribbean nations.

name: Branching Fire Coral
flavor: Branching Fire Coral ignites across the ground, its smooth pale arms radiating a searing sting that warns all who draw near.
fun_facts: Not a true coral but a hydrozoan — more closely related to jellyfish and Portuguese man o war.
Delivers a painful, burning sting on contact — the source of its common name.
Has two types of polyps: dactylozooids (for defense and feeding) and gastrozooids (for digestion).
One of the most important carbonate producers on Caribbean reefs despite not being a true coral.
Bleaches dramatically white when water temperatures rise, turning ghostly before recovering or dying.

name: Blade Fire Coral
flavor: Thin blades of Fire Coral slice upward like molten knives cooled mid-strike, their mustard-yellow edges concealing a venomous touch.
fun_facts: Forms thin, blade-like plates that orient perpendicular to prevailing currents to maximize food capture.
Like all fire corals, it can severely sting swimmers and divers who brush against it.
Can overgrow and kill true corals, sometimes dominating large sections of shallow reef.
Its calcium carbonate skeleton is very similar to true corals and contributes significantly to reef structure.
Colors range from mustard yellow to bright orange and bleach to stark white under heat stress.

name: Box Fire Coral
flavor: Angular slabs of Box Fire Coral lock together in blocky formations, each surface armed with invisible nematocysts eager to punish the unwary.
fun_facts: Forms distinctive box-like or angular encrusting colonies rather than blades or branches.
Found mainly in the Caribbean and tropical Atlantic.
Like other Millepora, it harbors symbiotic zooxanthellae that provide most energy via photosynthesis.
Its sting is caused by nematocysts similar to those of its jellyfish relatives.
Often encrusts dead gorgonians and other structural skeletons on the reef.

name: Bubble Coral
flavor: Bubble Coral swells into a cluster of translucent, grape-like vesicles, each one taut with water and shimmering with trapped light.
fun_facts: Inflates large, grape-like water-filled vesicles during the day that retract at night when tentacles emerge.
The bubbles serve a dual purpose: increasing surface area for zooxanthellae and deterring predators.
One of the most popular and recognizable corals in the marine aquarium trade.
Native to the Indo-Pacific, from the Red Sea to the central Pacific.
The bubble vesicles can burst if damaged, but typically reinflate within hours.

name: Pearl Bubble Coral
flavor: Clusters of Pearl Bubble Coral appear on a shaded wall, their small lustrous vesicles gleaming like a hoard of pearls set into living rock.
fun_facts: Similar to bubble coral but produces smaller, more numerous pearl-like vesicles.
Often found on shaded vertical reef faces and under overhangs in the Indo-Pacific.
The retracted night-time form looks completely different from the daytime bubble-inflated form.
Tentacles extended at night can stretch 5-10 cm to capture zooplankton.
Considered rare in many parts of its range and is listed on CITES Appendix II.

name: Elegance Coral
flavor: Elegance Coral unfurls from the sand, its enormous fleshy tentacles tipped in pink and white swaying with predatory grace.
fun_facts: Lives in sandy or muddy substrate — unusual for a large-polyped stony coral.
The polyp tissue is extremely large and fleshy with distinctive pink or white tentacle tip coloration.
Wildly popular in the aquarium trade, which has heavily impacted wild populations.
Found in the Indo-Pacific, particularly in sheltered lagoons and bays with soft substrate.
Tentacles contain powerful nematocysts used to sting and immobilize small fish and crustaceans.

name: Hammer Coral
flavor: Hammer Coral extends its anchor-tipped tentacles in a swaying curtain, each fleshy hammerhead poised to lash out at anything that encroaches.
fun_facts: Named for the anchor or hammer-shaped tips of its tentacles, which are unique among corals.
Extremely aggressive — its sweeper tentacles can reach over 15 cm and sting neighboring corals severely.
One of the most popular corals in reef aquariums worldwide due to its flowing movement.
Found across the Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea to Australia.
Listed on CITES Appendix II due to collection pressure from the aquarium trade.

name: Torch Coral
flavor: Torch Coral blazes to life, its long flowing tentacles streaming like living flames that sway and hunt in an invisible current.
fun_facts: Has long, flowing tentacles tipped with rounded ends that sway in the current like torches in a breeze.
Hosts commensal clownfish in the wild — the tentacles provide the same shelter as an anemone.
One of the most variable corals for tentacle color: green, gold, brown, pink, and bicolor morphs exist.
Actively hunts small zooplankton and even tiny fish at night.
A popular aquarium coral that can grow quite large in captivity, sometimes exceeding 30 cm across.

name: Flower Pot Coral
flavor: Flower Pot Coral erupts in a bouquet of impossibly long polyps, each one reaching outward like grasping fingers crowned with petals.
fun_facts: Has the longest polyps of any stony coral — individual polyps can extend up to 30 cm.
When extended, the colony resembles a pot of flowers with 24-tentacled daytime-active polyps.
Has a notorious reputation in the aquarium trade for being difficult to keep alive long-term.
Found in turbid, silty environments in the Indo-Pacific where few other corals thrive.
The colony structure contains hundreds of polyps all connected by living tissue.

name: Alveopora Coral
flavor: Alveopora Coral assembles itself from an open lattice of skeleton, its twelve-tentacled polyps blooming through the porous framework like stars through a trellis.
fun_facts: Similar to Goniopora but polyps have only 12 tentacles rather than 24.
Forms branching, knobby, or encrusting colonies depending on location and water flow.
Found mainly in the Red Sea, Arabian Gulf, and Indian Ocean.
Despite its delicate appearance, it is hardier in reef aquariums than its relative Goniopora.
The open skeletal framework provides habitat for small invertebrates and fish.

name: Blastomussa Coral
flavor: Blastomussa Coral clusters into a mound of swollen polyps, each one inflating like a fleshy grape in colors that shift from dawn to dusk.
fun_facts: Forms clusters of large, individual polyps on a shared skeleton — resembling a bunch of fleshy grapes.
Each polyp can inflate dramatically during the day and retract to a fraction of its size at night.
Tolerates lower light and water flow than most corals, making it suitable for dimmer tank positions.
Popular in the reef aquarium hobby due to its dramatic color variety and relative hardiness.
Found on lower reef slopes and in shaded environments across the Indo-Pacific.

name: Doughnut Coral
flavor: A single gargantuan polyp of Doughnut Coral inflates from a tiny skeleton, its translucent flesh ballooning outward in defiance of its stony core.
fun_facts: A solitary coral with one enormous fleshy polyp that can inflate to several times its skeleton size.
Often found living on soft substrate between rubble and coral on reef slopes.
The tissue contains high concentrations of zooxanthellae that give it vivid colors.
Extremely popular in reef aquariums — one of the most photographed and traded corals worldwide.
Despite its large size and bold appearance, it is a single polyp animal.

name: Solitary Disk Coral
flavor: A vivid disc of Solitary Disk Coral appears like a jewel pressed into rubble, its concentric rings of color daring the eye to look away.
fun_facts: A large, solitary coral disc up to 15 cm across, prized for vivid colors including red, orange, and green.
Found on rubble and hard substrate on deeper reef slopes in the Indo-Pacific.
Aquarium trade varieties from Australia are among the most expensive corals ever sold.
Unlike most large polyped stony corals, it spawns by broadcasting eggs and sperm into the water.
Uses sweeper tentacles to defend its territory from encroaching organisms.

name: Diploastrea Coral
flavor: Diploastrea Coral surfaces as a vast, impossibly smooth dome, a living fossil whose patience is measured in millennia rather than years.
fun_facts: The only species in its genus — a living fossil with no close living relatives.
Forms large, extremely smooth-surfaced domes — the smoothest of any faviid coral.
One of the slowest-growing massive corals, but individual colonies can live for over 1,000 years.
Extremely resistant to bleaching, and rarely observed bleached even during major thermal events.
Its growth rings are used by paleoclimatologists to reconstruct past ocean temperatures over centuries.

name: Brain Maze Coral
flavor: Brain Maze Coral manifests in an intricate whorl of shared walls and mouth grooves, a puzzle-box organism that has outlived dynasties.
fun_facts: Forms one of the most intricate maze-like surface patterns of any brain coral.
Extremely common on Indo-Pacific reefs from the Red Sea to the Pacific.
Colonies can exceed 1 meter in diameter and live for several centuries.
One of the most thermally tolerant corals in the Indo-Pacific.
The maze pattern is created by polyp rows that share walls and mouth grooves.

name: Lesser Star Coral
flavor: Lesser Star Coral encrusts the stone in a dense carpet of tiny polyp cups, glowing a spectral green as if lit from within by captured starlight.
fun_facts: Forms encrusting or domed colonies with tiny, closely packed polyp cups.
Often fluorescent green under blue light, making it glow dramatically on reef surveys.
Found from very shallow water to depths of 40 m across the Indo-Pacific.
One of the most common corals in Hawaii, where it carpets many inshore reef areas.
Produces a characteristic mucosal layer that helps protect it from UV radiation in shallow water.

name: Purple Leptastrea
flavor: Purple Leptastrea spreads in a flat, encrusting sheet of royal violet, colonizing bare stone with the quiet tenacity of something that endures all.
fun_facts: One of the few corals named for a color — purpurea referring to its characteristic purple-pink hues.
Highly adaptable, found in very shallow wave-swept zones as well as deeper slopes.
One of the few corals known to survive in extremely low-salinity intertidal pools.
Forms flat, encrusting sheets that can carpet large areas of inshore reef.
One of the first corals to recolonize bare substrate after disturbances.

name: Coscinarea Coral
flavor: Coscinarea Coral rises in coarsely ridged columns, its perforated skeletal plates stacking upward like the foundations of a submerged citadel.
fun_facts: Forms distinctive columnar or encrusting growth with a coarsely ridged surface.
The skeletal structure shows an unusual pattern of columns supporting a perforated plate.
Found from the Red Sea to the central Pacific in clear, well-lit reef environments.
Often hosts a distinctive community of commensal organisms on its rough surface.
A relatively understudied coral compared to more commercially important species.

name: Pencil Coral
flavor: Delicate stalks of Pencil Coral reach upward in pencil-thin formations, fragile as quills yet sharp enough to shelter the smallest creatures.
fun_facts: Forms delicate, pencil-thin branching colonies unlike the stout branches of true Acropora.
Found in sheltered lagoons and bays where water is calm enough for its fragile branches.
A rare and poorly studied genus with only about 10 species worldwide.
The thin branches provide very specific microhabitat for certain obligate coral-dwelling fish.
Listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List due to reef degradation across its range.

name: Bird's Nest Coral
flavor: A tangled mass of Bird's Nest Coral knits together from needle-thin branches, forming a dense thicket that dares intruders to reach inside.
fun_facts: Forms dense, tangled masses of fine branches resembling a bird's nest.
One of the most delicate branching corals — the needle-thin branches break extremely easily.
Provides critical dense habitat for small fish, shrimp, and crabs that shelter deep within the branches.
One of the fastest growing corals under ideal conditions, adding several cm of branch length per year.
Extremely sensitive to bleaching and among the first corals to die during thermal stress events.

name: Smooth Cauliflower Coral
flavor: Smooth Cauliflower Coral compacts itself into a rounded head of blunt-tipped branches, sturdy and methodical as a scholar among wilder kin.
fun_facts: One of the most studied corals in the world — a common subject of reef biology research.
Forms compact, rounded colonies of blunt-tipped branches resembling cauliflower.
Found from the Red Sea to the Pacific in a huge variety of colors and growth forms.
Has been used extensively to study coral calcification, bleaching, and symbiont biology.
One of the key corals used in reef restoration programs worldwide.

name: Cauliflower Coral
flavor: Cauliflower Coral springs forth in a burst of knobbly branches, already teeming with the commensal crabs and shrimp that call its thickets home.
fun_facts: Among the most widespread and common corals in the Indo-Pacific and eastern Pacific.
Often among the first corals to recolonize disturbed reef areas after bleaching or storms.
Harbors complex communities of obligate commensal crabs, shrimp, and fish within its branches.
Unusual in that it can reproduce both sexually and asexually by releasing brooded planula larvae.
Used extensively as a model organism in coral biology and climate change research.

name: Warty Coral
flavor: Warty Coral hardens from the ether, its prominent verrucae studding every branch like blisters on a gauntlet forged in brine.
fun_facts: Distinguished from other Pocillopora by its large, prominent verrucae (wart-like bumps) on branches.
One of the most thermally sensitive Pocillopora species, often among the first to bleach.
Found across the Indo-Pacific in exposed reef crest environments with high water flow.
The branch structure forms a complex microhabitat supporting hundreds of invertebrate species.
Spawns annually in synchrony with other coral species during seasonal mass-spawning events.

name: Capricorn Coral
flavor: Whorling vases of Capricorn Coral spiral open in vivid reds and purples, their rough surfaces catching the light like fired ceramic.
fun_facts: Forms whorling, vase-shaped or plating colonies with a characteristically rough surface texture.
Named capricornis for its original collection site near the Tropic of Capricorn.
A beginner-friendly aquarium coral — one of the hardiest and most forgiving Montipora species.
Often vivid red, orange, or purple — one of the more colorful reef corals.
Provides excellent substrate for settling coral larvae, contributing to natural reef recruitment.

name: Finger Montipora
flavor: Short, sturdy fingers of Montipora Coral cluster together in a compact stand, their dense spacing forming a miniature fortress of calcified digits.
fun_facts: Forms clusters of short, finger-like branches that give it a distinctive compact appearance.
One of the most common corals on Indo-Pacific reefs and widely available in the aquarium trade.
Grows quickly under good conditions and is used in reef restoration projects.
The small branch spacing creates dense microhabitat for tiny cryptic invertebrates.
Color varies widely — the same species can appear cream, brown, pink, purple, or bright orange.

name: Lettuce Coral
flavor: Lettuce Coral ruffles outward in undulating waves of living plate, each folded edge maximizing its hungry reach toward the light.
fun_facts: Forms wavy, undulating plates that resemble the ruffled leaves of a lettuce head.
Found across the Indo-Pacific on reef slopes from 1-20 m depth.
The wavy edge increases surface area, maximizing light exposure for its zooxanthellae.
Like other Montipora species, it grows relatively quickly and is used in reef restoration.
Color variants range from cream and tan to vivid purple and green.

name: Astreopora Coral
flavor: Astreopora Coral encrusts the terrain in a dome of ten thousand tiny pits, each one a watching eye in a sentinel of living stone.
fun_facts: Forms encrusting or domed colonies with a surface covered in tiny, closely spaced polyp pits.
Myriophthalma means ten thousand eyes — a reference to its densely pitted surface.
Found across the Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea to the Pacific.
Tolerates a range of water quality conditions including slightly turbid inshore environments.
Often grows over dead coral skeletons, encrusting and recycling them into living reef structure.

name: Blue Coral
flavor: Blue Coral solidifies with a skeleton stained permanent cerulean, a hundred-million-year-old design rendered anew in pigment and stone.
fun_facts: The only octocoral (8-tentacled polyp group) to build a massive calcium carbonate skeleton.
Its skeleton is permanently blue due to biliverdin, a bile pigment — the blue persists in dried museum specimens.
Found in the Indo-Pacific, especially common in the Philippines and Indonesia.
Has survived largely unchanged for over 100 million years — a genuine living fossil.
Listed on CITES Appendix II due to collection for the curio trade.

name: Organ Pipe Coral
flavor: Organ Pipe Coral assembles itself from parallel crimson tubes linked by horizontal platforms, like a pipe organ built for a cathedral beneath the waves.
fun_facts: Forms a skeleton of parallel bright red tubes connected by horizontal platforms, resembling a pipe organ.
An octocoral (soft coral relative) despite producing a hard, permanent skeleton.
The red color of the skeleton is permanent and comes from iron salts.
Individual polyps are bright green with 8 feathery tentacles.
Has been historically collected for the curio trade; now listed on CITES Appendix II.

name: Dead Man's Fingers
flavor: Pale, bloated lobes of Dead Man's Fingers swell from the rock like the hand of a drowned giant clawing upward from its grave.
fun_facts: A temperate soft coral from the northeastern Atlantic and North Sea — not a tropical species.
Named for its pale, swollen lobes which resemble bloated fingers, especially when retracted.
Can cover large areas of rocky seafloor in northern European coastal waters.
Unlike tropical soft corals, it has no symbiotic algae — it feeds entirely on plankton.
Produces chemical compounds that deter fish and sea urchins from grazing on it.

name: Flexible Leather Coral
flavor: Flexible Leather Coral bends into existence with a toxic sigh, its rubbery lobes exuding alchemical compounds that wither all rivals nearby.
fun_facts: One of the most dominant soft corals on Indo-Pacific reefs, sometimes covering vast areas of the reef slope.
Produces powerful toxic compounds (sinulariolide) that kill neighboring hard corals and prevent overgrowth.
Despite its toxicity to other corals, it supports communities of obligate soft-coral-dwelling fish.
One of the most commonly kept soft corals in reef aquariums due to its hardy nature.
After storms, fragments reattach and regrow, allowing rapid recovery of populations.

name: Toadstool Coral
flavor: A broad Toadstool Coral rises on a thick stalk, its ruffled cap unfurling like a parasol over the battlefield as it sheds its waxy skin.
fun_facts: Has a distinctive mushroom or toadstool shape with a thick stalk and broad, ruffled cap.
One of the most popular and hardy soft corals in the reef aquarium hobby.
Regularly sheds a waxy coat from its surface to remove algae and sediment.
Produces terpene compounds that are being studied for potential pharmaceutical applications.
Can grow very large — colonies in the wild can exceed 50 cm across.

name: Thick Leather Coral
flavor: Thick Leather Coral spreads in heavy, lobed masses across the ground, its surface alternating between velvety softness and smooth menace as polyps withdraw.
fun_facts: Forms thick, encrusting lobed masses that can cover several square meters of reef.
One of the dominant soft corals on Indo-Pacific reef flats and upper slopes.
Like other leather corals, it produces allelopathic (neighbor-killing) chemicals.
Polyps are retractile — the colony can appear completely smooth when polyps are withdrawn.
Targeted by nudibranch predators that are specifically adapted to feed on Lobophytum.

name: Cauliflower Soft Coral
flavor: Bushy heads of Cauliflower Soft Coral burst upward in pale clusters, tiny white polyps opening across every surface like fresh snow on broccoli.
fun_facts: Forms bushy, cauliflower-like colonies of clustered branches bearing tiny white polyps.
One of the fastest-colonizing soft corals after reef disturbances.
Produces chemical compounds that have shown antibacterial properties in laboratory studies.
Found across the Indo-Pacific in a wide range of reef environments.
Despite being soft-bodied, the colony contains tiny calcium carbonate spicules for structural support.

name: Pulsing Xenia
flavor: Pulsing Xenia blooms in rhythmic waves, its feathery tentacles opening and closing in a hypnotic cadence as though conducting an unheard symphony.
fun_facts: Famous for rhythmically pulsing its feathery tentacles — one of the most mesmerizing behaviors on the reef.
The pulsing motion enhances gas exchange and brings food-laden water to the polyps.
Unusually, it derives most energy from photosynthesis rather than filter feeding.
Can reproduce so rapidly in reef aquariums that it is considered a nuisance weed by some hobbyists.
Scientists have puzzled for decades over why it pulses — the exact function is still debated.

name: Fuscescens Xenia
flavor: Stalked clusters of Fuscescens Xenia pulse with a subtly different rhythm than their cousins, their movement a whispered counterpoint in the current.
fun_facts: Also pulses rhythmically like pulsing xenia, but the motion is subtly different in timing.
Forms clusters of tall, stalked polyp heads on carbonate substrates.
Common in the Red Sea and Indian Ocean, where it can dominate shallow reef flats.
One of the few animals known to rely on photosynthesis for essentially all of its energy needs.
Reproduces rapidly by budding and can form dense meadows on degraded reefs.

name: Efflatounaria Coral
flavor: Thin fingers of Efflatounaria Coral reach outward in a bushy spray, an enigmatic organism still half-unknown to even the most learned scholars.
fun_facts: A poorly studied genus of soft coral found mainly in the Red Sea and Indian Ocean.
Forms bushy colonies with thin, finger-like branches.
Named after Egyptian zoologist Ahmed Efflatoun, who described many Red Sea invertebrates.
Likely produces allelopathic chemicals but these have not been well characterized scientifically.
Its taxonomy is still being revised as molecular tools are applied to soft coral classification.

name: Clove Polyp Coral
flavor: A living mat of Clove Polyp Coral unfurls across the stone, each tiny eight-armed polyp a bright green snowflake in an ever-spreading carpet.
fun_facts: Forms mats of individual polyps that resemble tiny cloves or snowflakes with eight feathery tentacles.
Bright green coloration due to symbiotic zooxanthellae and fluorescent proteins.
Spreads by extending stolons (runners) across the substrate, which develop new polyps.
A popular beginner soft coral in reef aquariums due to its hardiness and fast growth.
Each polyp is an individual organism connected to its neighbors by a thin mat of living tissue.

name: Anthelia Soft Coral
flavor: Tall, graceful polyps of Anthelia Soft Coral sway into being, their feathered arms waving slowly like acolytes in a silent underwater procession.
fun_facts: Forms mats of tall, graceful polyps that sway gently in the current.
Found in the Red Sea and Indo-Pacific in moderate to high current environments.
Unlike pulsing xenia, Anthelia polyps do not pulse — they simply wave in the current.
One of the most graceful-looking soft corals on the reef, often misidentified as an anemone.
The feathery tentacles trap plankton and detritus from the water column.

name: Tree Soft Coral
flavor: A towering Tree Soft Coral rises like an underwater oak, its spicule-stiffened branches forming a canopy in hues of gold, pink, and crimson.
fun_facts: Forms tree-like branching colonies that can grow over a meter tall, creating an underwater forest.
Non-photosynthetic — relies entirely on filter feeding for nutrition.
The branches are stiffened by calcium carbonate spicules embedded in the fleshy tissue.
One of the dominant soft corals in the Indo-Pacific, particularly in areas with strong currents.
Dazzlingly colorful — found in yellow, orange, pink, red, and white varieties.

name: Broccoli Coral
flavor: Dense, rounded heads of Broccoli Coral cluster together in a verdant mound, concealing within their branches a pharmacy of potent terpenoids.
fun_facts: Resembles a head of broccoli — dense, rounded clusters of polyp branches.
Very common in the Red Sea, where it can dominate large sections of reef slope.
Non-photosynthetic and feeds entirely on plankton.
Produces a vast array of terpenoid compounds being studied as potential anti-cancer agents.
The colony is supported internally by a forest of calcium carbonate spicules.

name: Carnation Coral
flavor: Carnation Coral explodes into view in a riot of scarlet, tangerine, and rose, its translucent flesh revealing the glittering spicules within like jewels beneath glass.
fun_facts: Among the most spectacularly colorful animals in the ocean — vivid red, orange, pink, yellow, and white.
Non-photosynthetic and requires very high plankton levels — notoriously difficult in aquariums.
The internal spicules are clearly visible through the translucent tissue.
Found in areas of strong current where plankton is constantly delivered to its polyps.
Often highlighted in nature documentaries as an example of extreme reef biodiversity.

name: Stereonephthya Coral
flavor: Stereonephthya Coral solidifies into a rigid, compact cluster, its granular spicules visible through pale tissue like sand trapped in amber.
fun_facts: Similar in appearance to Dendronephthya but with more rigid, compact colony structure.
Found in the Indo-Pacific in high-flow environments.
Non-photosynthetic filter feeder that requires consistent plankton-rich water.
The spicules in each branch can be seen as a granular texture through the tissue.
Taxonomy is still poorly resolved — many species remain undescribed by science.

name: Chili Coral
flavor: Vivid clusters of Chili Coral dangle from a darkened overhang, each polyp group a small ember of red burning in the gloom of a cave wall.
fun_facts: Forms small, compact clusters of vivid red or orange polyp groups — resembling chili peppers.
Non-photosynthetic and strictly filter-feeding, requiring strong currents.
Often found on cave walls and under overhangs where light levels are very low.
The brilliant colors come from carotenoid pigments rather than algae or fluorescent proteins.
A highly sought-after coral in the aquarium trade but very difficult to keep without live plankton.

name: Gorgonian Sea Fan
flavor: A broad Gorgonian Sea Fan spreads wide across the current, its gorgonin skeleton flexing as thousands of tiny polyps extend their feathered arms to feed.
fun_facts: Forms a two-dimensional fan-like colony oriented perpendicular to the current to maximize food capture.
The fan structure is supported by a flexible internal axial skeleton of gorgonin protein.
Tiny polyps along the branches extend feathery tentacles to capture passing plankton.
Can grow very large — some fans exceed 2 meters across.
The internal skeleton has been historically used to make jewelry and art objects.

name: Purple Sea Fan
flavor: An iconic Purple Sea Fan unfurls perpendicular to an invisible tide, its latticed violet branches filtering the water like a net woven from amethyst.
fun_facts: The iconic purple sea fan of the Caribbean — a flagship species of Caribbean reef imagery.
Always orients its fan perpendicular to prevailing currents for maximum filter-feeding efficiency.
Hosts the flamingo tongue snail (Cyphoma gibbosum), which grazes on its tissue leaving distinctive scars.
Sea fans have been historically overharvested for use in jewelry and as wall decorations.
A key indicator species for Caribbean reef health assessments.

name: Venus Sea Fan
flavor: A lace-fine Venus Sea Fan appears on the reef wall, its delicate tracery bending dramatically in the surge without ever breaking.
fun_facts: Forms a finely branched, lace-like fan structure more delicate than the purple sea fan.
Can grow on vertical walls as well as on horizontal reef surfaces.
Found in shallower water than many gorgonians — sometimes in as little as 3 m depth.
The fan skeleton is flexible — it bends dramatically in surge and current without breaking.
Suffers from aspergillosis, a fungal disease that has killed large portions of Caribbean populations.

name: Knobby Sea Rod
flavor: Upright rods of Knobby Sea Rod spring from the substrate, their knobbly polyp bases studding each branch like rivets on a column of living leather.
fun_facts: Named for the prominent knob-like bases of its polyp calyces along the branches.
Forms upright, rod-like colonies that branch irregularly, creating a bushy structure.
A common and important soft coral on Caribbean reefs, providing habitat for many invertebrates.
The flexible skeleton bends in surge but springs back — it rarely breaks in storms.
Produces bioactive compounds including pseudopterosins, being studied as anti-inflammatory drugs.

name: Sea Plume
flavor: A towering Sea Plume sways into existence, its feathered fronds heavy with prostaglandins that seep into the water like a druid's bitter offering.
fun_facts: One of the most abundant gorgonians on Caribbean reefs, creating dense sea plume gardens.
Famous as the source of prostaglandin-like compounds discovered in the 1960s — a landmark in biochemistry.
Produces up to 8% of its dry weight in prostaglandins — more than any other organism known.
Colonies can grow over a meter tall and live for decades on the reef.
The discovery of its prostaglandins revolutionized research into these important biological signaling molecules.

name: Slit-Pore Sea Rod
flavor: Thick, sparsely branched rods of Slit-Pore Sea Rod stand like sentinels, their distinctive slit-shaped openings hissing faintly in the current.
fun_facts: Named for the distinctive slit-shaped (rather than round) openings of its polyp calyces.
Forms tall, sparsely branched colonies of thick rods.
Found across the Caribbean and tropical Atlantic.
Like other gorgonians, it orients branches to maximize exposure to water flow for filter feeding.
Hosts a diverse community of small crustaceans and worms within its branches.

name: Feather Bush Coral
flavor: Lush fronds of Feather Bush Coral cascade outward in a plume of fine branches, their tissues laced with potent compounds that make even the water sting.
fun_facts: Forms feather-like fronds of fine branches that create lush underwater gardens.
A major producer of pseudopterosins — natural compounds with potent anti-inflammatory properties.
Now used commercially: pseudopterosin is extracted for use in cosmetics and skin care products.
Can grow over a meter tall on shallow Caribbean reefs.
One of the best-studied gorgonians due to its pharmaceutical importance.

name: Orange Sea Fan
flavor: A broad Orange Sea Fan stretches across the current in sunset hues, its surface so finely textured that pygmy creatures vanish against it entirely.
fun_facts: Forms broad, orange to red fans in the Indo-Pacific and West Pacific.
A non-photosynthetic gorgonian that requires strong currents for filter feeding.
Often found on current-swept walls and channels where food availability is high.
Hosts commensal pygmy seahorses (Hippocampus bargibanti) that precisely match its color and texture.
The association with pygmy seahorses makes Muricella fans prized by underwater photographers.

name: Melithaea Fan Coral
flavor: Melithaea Fan Coral flexes into view on alternating hard and soft nodes, its scarlet fan a banner planted on bare rock where nothing else will grow.
fun_facts: Produces bright red, orange, or pink fans in the Indo-Pacific.
The skeleton has alternating hard and flexible nodes — a distinctive feature of the Melithaeidae family.
Non-photosynthetic, relying entirely on filter feeding.
Found in strong current areas from shallow reefs to deeper mesophotic environments.
The colorful fans provide important structure on rocky walls that would otherwise be bare.

name: Bamboo Coral
flavor: Bamboo Coral rises in segmented lengths of white calcite and dark protein, bending like a martial artist's staff in the invisible tides of magic.
fun_facts: Has an unmistakable skeleton of alternating white calcified internodes and dark flexible nodes — just like bamboo.
The flexible nodes allow the colony to bend dramatically in current without breaking.
Found from shallow reefs to very deep water — related deep-sea species live at 1,000+ m depth.
Can grow over 2 meters tall on Indo-Pacific reefs.
The white calcified portions are pure calcium carbonate while the dark nodes are gorgonin protein.

name: Black Coral
flavor: Black Coral coils upward from the deep, its dark chitin skeleton ancient as superstition itself, crowned by polyps of startling gold.
fun_facts: Black corals have been symbols of good luck in Hawaiian and Caribbean cultures for centuries.
The internal skeleton is black or dark brown — made of an organic chitin-like protein, not calcium carbonate.
Found from shallow water to extreme depths — some species have been found at over 8,000 meters.
Despite their name, the living polyps are often vivid yellow, orange, or white.
Hawaii has the largest black coral fishery in the US; the coral is protected in many other jurisdictions.

name: Wire Coral
flavor: A single spiraling strand of Wire Coral extends from the rock like a conjured whip, tiny polyps bristling along its length in a fuzzy helix.
fun_facts: Forms a single unbranched strand that spirals and can grow to over 2 meters long.
Tiny polyps line the length of the wire, giving it a fuzzy appearance up close.
Hosts obligate commensal shrimp and tiny gobies (Bryaninops spp.) that live exclusively on wire corals.
The spiral shape helps keep the coral upright in current without a broad fan structure.
Some wire corals can live for decades, slowly extending their single strand across the reef.

name: Pink Lace Coral
flavor: Delicate Pink Lace Coral crystallizes on a shaded wall, its rose-tinted fan as fine and treacherous as spun glass hiding a venomous secret.
fun_facts: A hydrocoral like fire coral, but delicate and lace-like rather than massive or branching.
Forms stunning pink or purple fan-like structures on shaded reef walls and in caves.
Like fire coral, it can deliver a mild sting — surprising given its delicate appearance.
Found in the Caribbean and tropical Atlantic, usually in shaded or low-light environments.
Listed on CITES Appendix II — heavily collected in the past for the curio trade.

name: Violet Hydrocoral
flavor: Violet Hydrocoral branches into a vivid purple fan on a darkened overhang, its color so saturated it seems to bleed pigment into the surrounding shadow.
fun_facts: Forms delicate, violet to purple branching fans — among the most colorful of all reef invertebrates.
A stylasterid hydrocoral — more closely related to fire coral and jellyfish than to true corals.
Found on shaded vertical walls and overhangs across the Indo-Pacific.
The violet color is exceptionally vivid and stable — it does not fade quickly after collection.
Like all stylasterid hydrocorals, it feeds entirely by filter feeding with no photosynthetic symbiont.
